meta.source: General knowledge of typical published cost-of-travel ranges. Not a live pricing or FX API.
meta.how_to_edit: Every daily figure is US dollars, per person, per day. Flight figures are US dollars for one round-trip ticket per person from that departure region. Change a number, save the file, reload the page.
meta.rounding: Daily figures rounded to the nearest 5 USD (or nearest 1 USD for the very cheapest lines). Flights rounded to the nearest 50 USD.
meta.sharing_rule: When travellers share rooms the app prices a double room at 1.4x the listed per-person rate, i.e. about 30% off each. Dorm beds (Backpacker tier) are already per-person, so sharing does not change them.

tiers.label: Backpacker
tiers.description: Hostel dorms, street food and self-catering, public buses, mostly free activities.

tiers.label: Budget
tiers.description: Private hostel rooms or cheap guesthouses, local restaurants, the occasional taxi, some paid attractions.

tiers.label: Mid-range
tiers.description: 3-star hotels or good Airbnbs, a mix of restaurants, comfortable transport, regular paid activities.

tiers.label: Luxury
tiers.description: 4/5-star hotels, fine dining, private transfers and domestic flights, premium tours.

countries.name: Morocco
notes: Best weather April-May and September-October; high summer is punishing inland.
Cash still rules in the medinas, and small tips (5-10 dirham) are expected almost everywhere.

countries.name: Egypt
notes: October-April is the season; summer in Luxor and Aswan regularly passes 40C.
Baksheesh tipping is constant - carry a wad of small pound notes. The pound has devalued sharply, so local-currency figures move fast.

countries.name: South Africa
notes: December-January is the domestic holiday peak on the coast; the Cape is best November-March.
Cards work almost everywhere and a 10% restaurant tip is standard. Private game lodges sit well above even the Luxury figures here.

countries.name: Tunisia
notes: June-August is beach peak; spring and autumn are far more comfortable for the Sahara and the ruins.
The dinar is a closed currency - you cannot buy it before you arrive or take it home. Cash for souks, cards in resorts.

countries.name: Algeria
notes: Most nationalities need a visa arranged in advance, often with a local invitation or tour booking.
A cash economy with unreliable foreign-card ATMs, and a parallel exchange rate that differs a lot from the official one - treat the dinar figures as rough.

countries.name: Kenya
notes: July-October is the Mara migration peak and prices reflect it; the long rains are March-May.
M-Pesa mobile money is used for everything. National park fees are priced in US dollars and are the single biggest activity cost.

countries.name: Tanzania
notes: June-October dry season is peak for the Serengeti and Kilimanjaro.
Serengeti and Ngorongoro entry fees are steep and quoted in US dollars. Zanzibar is much cheaper than a mainland safari.

countries.name: Zimbabwe
countries.currency_name: US dollar (used in practice alongside the ZiG)
notes: Victoria Falls is at its fullest February-May; wildlife viewing is best August-October.
US dollars are used for nearly everything - bring clean, small bills, as change is a genuine problem and card acceptance is patchy.

countries.name: Uganda
notes: Drier windows are June-August and December-February, though Uganda is green year-round.
A gorilla trekking permit is a fixed one-off of roughly USD 800 per person on top of these daily figures - add it separately if you plan to go.

countries.name: Namibia
countries.currency_name: Namibian dollar (pegged 1:1 to the South African rand)
notes: A self-drive country - a 4x4 or high-clearance rental plus fuel is usually the largest line in the budget, which is why transport is high here.
May-October is the dry season and best for wildlife. South African rand is accepted at par.

countries.name: China
notes: Avoid Golden Week (first week of October) and Chinese New Year - domestic travel is close to impossible.
Cash is nearly obsolete. Link a foreign card to Alipay or WeChat Pay before you fly or you will struggle to pay for anything.

countries.name: Thailand
notes: November-February is the cool dry peak; the islands have opposite monsoons on each coast.
Tipping is not expected but rounding up is normal. Cards are fine in cities, cash on the islands and at markets.

countries.name: Japan
notes: Cherry blossom (late March to mid-April) and autumn colour (November) are peak - book accommodation months ahead.
No tipping anywhere, ever. Get an IC card (Suica/ICOCA) for transport, and keep some cash for smaller restaurants.

countries.name: Malaysia
notes: The east coast islands (Perhentians, Tioman) largely close November-February for the monsoon.
Cards are widely accepted, tipping is not a thing, and hawker food keeps the food line very low.

countries.name: Vietnam
notes: The country is 1,600 km long and the north and south have opposite seasons - there is no single best month for the whole trip.
Cash still rules at street level. Tipping is not expected outside tourist restaurants.

countries.name: India
notes: October-March is the comfortable window across most of the country; April-June is extreme heat and July-September is monsoon.
UPI and cards work well in cities; keep cash for trains, rickshaws and markets. Around 10% is a normal restaurant tip.

countries.name: Indonesia
notes: Bali peaks in July-August and over Christmas; the wet season is roughly November-March.
Cash for warungs and scooter hire. ATM fees are per-withdrawal, so take out larger amounts less often.

countries.name: South Korea
notes: Spring (April) and autumn (October) are the best and the busiest; summer is hot, humid and wet.
No tipping. A T-money card covers buses, subways and many taxis, and cards are accepted virtually everywhere.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
countries.currency_name: Saudi riyal (pegged to the US dollar)
notes: November-March only - summer temperatures make sightseeing genuinely unsafe.
Alcohol is illegal, so budget nothing for it. Cards are near-universal, and modest dress is required.

countries.name: United Arab Emirates
countries.currency_name: UAE dirham (pegged to the US dollar)
notes: November-March is the season; July-August is 45C and everything happens indoors.
Alcohol is heavily taxed and hotel-only - a beer can be USD 12-15, which is enough to distort a food budget.

countries.name: France
notes: July-August is peak everywhere, and a lot of Paris genuinely shuts for August.
Service is included in restaurant bills - leaving small change is plenty. Cards are accepted almost universally.

countries.name: Spain
notes: July-August is coastal peak and inland heat; May-June and September are much better value.
Dinner starts around 21:00, and tipping is minimal - rounding up the bill is normal.

countries.name: Italy
notes: June-August is hot and crowded - major museums and the Vatican need booking well ahead.
A coperto (cover charge) on restaurant bills is normal; tipping beyond that is not expected.

countries.name: Turkey
notes: April-June and September-October are the sweet spots; the coast is packed in July-August.
High inflation means lira prices move fast - treat the local-currency figures here as rougher than for most countries.

countries.name: Germany
notes: Oktoberfest (late September) and the December Christmas markets spike hotel prices in Munich, Berlin and Nuremberg.
Cash is still expected in many bakeries, bars and small restaurants - do not assume your card will work.

countries.name: United Kingdom
notes: London runs roughly a third dearer than the rest of the country - basing yourself elsewhere changes the total a lot.
Contactless cards work on all London transport. Tip about 10% for table service only; never in pubs.

countries.name: Greece
notes: July-August island prices can double and ferries sell out; May-June and September are far better value.
Carry cash on smaller islands - card acceptance thins out quickly away from the main towns.

countries.name: Austria
notes: Two separate peaks: summer sightseeing, and the December-March ski season when Alpine prices jump sharply.
Round bills up by 5-10%. Cash is still common in rural guesthouses.

countries.name: Portugal
notes: Lisbon, Porto and the Algarve are busiest June-September; spring and autumn are mild and much cheaper.
Tipping is light. Cards are accepted but small cafes often have a card minimum, so keep coins.

countries.name: Netherlands
notes: Amsterdam hotel prices dominate the budget - Haarlem, Utrecht or Rotterdam cut accommodation sharply and are 20-40 minutes by train.
Many places are card-only, and some still refuse foreign credit cards - a debit card with Maestro is the safe bet.

countries.name: United States
notes: Tipping 18-20% on table service is not optional, and sales tax is added at the till - budget roughly 25% above menu and shelf prices.
Outside a handful of big cities a rental car is effectively mandatory, which is why the transport line is high.

countries.name: Mexico
notes: The Riviera Maya peaks December-April; the interior (Oaxaca, Mexico City) is pleasant most of the year.
Cash for markets and colectivos. Tipping 10-15% in restaurants is standard, and pay in pesos rather than dollars.

countries.name: Canada
notes: June-August is peak, and Banff/Jasper in July is the most expensive week of the Canadian year.
Tipping 15-20% plus taxes added at the till, exactly like the US. Distances are big - factor in a car or internal flights.

countries.name: Dominican Republic
notes: December-April is the dry peak; August-October carries real hurricane risk.
These figures assume independent travel. An all-inclusive package changes the maths completely and is often cheaper for a beach week.

countries.name: Cuba
notes: Bring every dollar you need as cash (euros or US dollars) - most foreign cards do not work, and US-issued cards do not work at all.
The informal exchange rate is wildly different from the official one, so the Cuban peso figures here are the roughest in this dataset. Casas particulares are the standard accommodation.

countries.name: Costa Rica
notes: December-April is dry season and peak pricing; the green season is cheaper and still perfectly workable.
US dollars are accepted almost everywhere, and 10% service plus 13% tax is usually already on restaurant bills.

countries.name: Jamaica
notes: December-April is peak; September-October is hurricane season and much quieter.
US dollars are widely accepted but you get poor value - pay in Jamaican dollars. Route taxis are a fraction of the cost of resort transfers.

countries.name: Panama
countries.currency_name: US dollar (the balboa is pegged 1:1 and only exists as coins)
notes: The US dollar is the working currency, so there is no conversion to think about.
December-April is dry season. Trips to San Blas and Bocas del Toro are cash-only and add a few hundred dollars quickly.

countries.name: Guatemala
notes: November-April is dry season; Semana Santa in Antigua is the single busiest and priciest week of the year.
Carry quetzal cash for shuttles and markets - ATMs are scarce outside Antigua, Xela and the capital.

countries.name: Bahamas
countries.currency_name: Bahamian dollar (pegged 1:1 to the US dollar)
notes: One of the most expensive destinations in the Americas - nearly all food and fuel is imported. There is essentially no backpacker infrastructure.
US and Bahamian dollars circulate interchangeably at 1:1. December-April is peak; ferries between the Out Islands need planning.

countries.name: Argentina
notes: Inflation is extreme and the peso figures here will drift within months - the US dollar amounts are the more reliable half.
Patagonia is only really open November-March, and Buenos Aires is pleasant in spring and autumn.

countries.name: Brazil
notes: Carnival (February or March) and New Year in Rio can triple accommodation - book six months out or avoid entirely.
Pix and cards are used everywhere and 10% service is usually printed on the bill. The country is huge, so budget for internal flights.

countries.name: Chile
notes: Patagonia and Torres del Paine are November-March only, and refugio beds inside the park need booking months ahead.
Cards work well in cities; carry cash further south and in the Atacama. Chile is noticeably pricier than its Andean neighbours.

countries.name: Peru
notes: May-September is the Andean dry season and the trekking window; the coast is best December-March.
Machu Picchu tickets and the Inca Trail sell out months ahead and are a large one-off cost on top of the daily figures.

countries.name: Colombia
notes: December-March is driest; Cartagena runs far pricier than Medellin or Bogota and skews any national average.
Cash is normal outside the big cities, and ATM withdrawal limits are low - expect several trips.

countries.name: Uruguay
notes: Noticeably pricier than Argentina or Brazil. Punta del Este in January is a different price bracket entirely.
Cards are widely used, and foreign visitors get the VAT refunded automatically on restaurant bills paid by foreign card.

countries.name: Ecuador
notes: The US dollar is the official currency - bring small bills, as change for USD 20 notes is often hard to find.
The Galapagos are a completely separate budget: park fee, transit card and a flight from the mainland before you spend a cent on the islands.

countries.name: Bolivia
notes: One of the cheapest countries in the Americas. May-October is dry season; the Uyuni salt flats mirror effect needs the wet season (January-March).
Cash is essential - card acceptance is limited outside La Paz and Santa Cruz, and US dollar cash is a useful backup.

countries.name: Paraguay
notes: Very little tourism infrastructure - expect few hostels and more small mid-range hotels, which lifts the bottom tier slightly.
May-September is cooler; summer regularly hits 40C. A cash-heavy economy outside Asuncion.

countries.name: Venezuela
countries.currency_name: US dollar (used in practice; the bolivar is hyperinflated)
notes: Check your government's travel advice before booking - much of the country is currently advised against, and insurance may not cover you.
The economy runs on US dollar cash in practice; bolivar prices are meaningless within weeks, so these figures are the least certain in the dataset.

countries.name: Australia
notes: Distances are enormous - domestic flights or a campervan are usually unavoidable and sit outside the local transport line for short trips.
December-January is the domestic holiday peak. No tipping expected, and cards are accepted everywhere including on buses.

countries.name: New Zealand
notes: Campervan or car hire dominates the transport line - public transport between towns is thin.
December-February is peak and books out well ahead. No tipping culture, and adventure activities (bungy, glacier heli) are the real budget risk.

countries.name: Fiji
notes: May-October is the dry season and the peak; November-April is cyclone season.
Island transfers by boat or light plane are a genuine cost line, and resorts commonly add a service charge plus government levies of around 15% in total.

countries.name: French Polynesia
notes: One of the most expensive destinations anywhere. Pensions de famille (family guesthouses) are the only real budget option - there is almost no hostel scene.
May-October is the dry season. Nearly everything is imported, so supermarket prices are roughly double mainland France.

countries.name: Papua New Guinea
notes: Hard and expensive to travel independently - domestic flights and local guides carry the budget, and security advice matters in Port Moresby and Lae.
May-October is drier. Cash outside the capital, and card acceptance is limited even in it.

countries.name: New Caledonia
notes: French prices in the Pacific - imported supermarket food is expensive, and Noumea restaurants are priced like Paris.
September-November is the pleasant shoulder. A hire car is near-essential on Grande Terre, which pushes the transport line up.

countries.name: Vanuatu
notes: April-October is the dry season; cyclone season runs November-April.
The Tanna and Ambrym volcano trips are a significant one-off cost, and inter-island flights are frequently rescheduled - build in slack days.

countries.name: Samoa
notes: Beach fales (simple open-sided huts) are the budget classic and usually include breakfast and dinner, which pulls the food line down.
May-October is dry season. Sundays are strictly observed and almost everything closes - plan around it.

countries.name: Cook Islands
notes: New Zealand dollars are the currency (with local coins). May-October is the dry season.
Rarotonga has one ring road and two bus routes, clockwise and anti-clockwise, so local transport stays cheap; Aitutaki day trips are the big spend.

countries.name: Tonga
notes: Humpback whale swimming (July-October) is the main draw and the main cost - a licensed day trip is a few hundred dollars.
Sundays are constitutionally protected: almost nothing opens. A cash-heavy economy with limited ATMs outside Nuku'alofa.
